final_text: With Redis, overwriting a key with SET clears its TTL. Write SET key value EX 30 (or SET followed by EXPIRE) on every heartbeat, or the key never expires. Since Redis 2.6 the expiry error is 0-1 ms.
note: Opened redis.io EXPIRE: 'The timeout will only be cleared by commands that delete or overwrite the contents of the key, including DEL, SET, GETSET'; 'Since Redis 2.6 the expire error is from 0 to 1 milliseconds.' The page's own example shows TTL -1 after a plain SET.

final_text: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items 'typically within a few days', and until then they are still returned by reads. Store an epoch-seconds expiry attribute and treat expiry < now as offline (use filter expressions on Query and Scan).
note: Opened DynamoDB TTL guide: expired items 'might be deleted by the system at any time, typically within a few days after their expiration'; 'Use filter expressions to remove expired items from Scan and Query results' (so they are still returned until deleted); attribute is a Number in Unix epoch seconds.

final_text: Redis expires keys two ways: passively, when a client accesses an expired key, and actively, by periodically testing random keys that have a TTL and deleting expired ones.
note: Opened redis.io EXPIRE appendix: 'Redis keys are expired in two ways: a passive way and an active way'; 'periodically, Redis tests a few keys at random amongst the set of keys with an expiration.'

final_text: DynamoDB TTL deletions do not consume write throughput, and they appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions, distinct from user deletes. An archival consumer can therefore tell expiries apart from explicit deletes.
note: Opened DynamoDB TTL guide: deletes happen 'without consuming write throughput'; 'items go into DynamoDB Streams as service deletions instead of user deletes'. Caveat: with global tables the replicated TTL delete does consume replicated write units in replica regions.

final_text: Debezium's MySQL connector reads the MySQL binlog and produces row-level change events that it publishes to Kafka topics.
note: Opened Debezium MySQL connector docs (3.7 latest stable): 'The Debezium MySQL connector reads the binlog, produces change events for row-level ... operations, and emits the change events to Kafka topics.'

final_text: PostgreSQL's INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is an atomic upsert: it inserts the row or updates the existing one, even under high concurrency. It covers the first heartbeat of a user with no row yet.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 INSERT: 'ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE guarantees an atomic INSERT or UPDATE outcome; provided there is no independent error, one of those two outcomes is guaranteed, even under high concurrency.' Needs a unique index/constraint as the conflict target.

final_text: A 4-byte epoch-seconds timestamp runs out in 2038: MySQL's TIMESTAMP type has a range of '1970-01-01 00:00:01' to '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC. New schemas should use 8-byte timestamps.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 datetime page: 'TIMESTAMP has a range of '1970-01-01 00:00:01' UTC to '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC.' Overlaps A-D-20 (attached to the wrong-verdict item L-0232); keep one prominently.

final_text: Each PostgreSQL row carries a 23-byte header (padded to 24 bytes on most machines) plus a 4-byte item pointer in its page, so a row with an 8-byte payload takes roughly 36 bytes on disk before any index, several times the raw payload.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 page layout: header 'occupying 23 bytes on most machines'; item identifiers '4 bytes per item'; user data starts at t_hoff, which 'must always be a multiple of the MAXALIGN distance'. 24 + 8 + 4 = 36, so 'about 40 bytes' overstated it slightly; reworded.

final_text: The Redis benchmark docs show example runs of about 180,000 SET requests/s on one instance without pipelining, and about 1.5 million/s with 16-command pipelining (that run on a MacBook Air); real numbers depend on hardware and payload. 100k small heartbeat writes/s is within one Redis node's range.
note: Opened redis.io benchmarks: example output 'SET: 180180.17 requests per second'; 'running the benchmark in a MacBook Air 11" using a pipelining of 16 commands: SET: 1536098.25 requests per second'. Reworded to present them as example runs on unspecified/laptop hardware, not guarantees.

final_text: HikariCP's connectionTimeout (default 30 s) is how long a caller waits for a free pooled connection before getting an error. maximumPoolSize (default 10) caps idle plus in-use connections.
note: Opened HikariCP README: connectionTimeout 'controls the maximum number of milliseconds that a client ... will wait for a connection from the pool', SQLException thrown on timeout, default 30000; maximumPoolSize 'including both idle and in-use connections', default 10.

final_text: HikariCP's idleTimeout (default 10 minutes) retires idle connections, but only when minimumIdle is below maximumPoolSize. maxLifetime (default 30 minutes) retires every connection after a fixed age.
note: Opened HikariCP README: idleTimeout 'only applies when minimumIdle is defined to be less than maximumPoolSize', default 600000 (10 min); maxLifetime 'maximum lifetime of a connection in the pool', default 1800000 (30 min).

final_text: HikariCP recommends not setting minimumIdle, so the pool acts as a fixed-size pool (minimum = maximum); its default minimumIdle equals maximumPoolSize.
note: Opened HikariCP README: minimumIdle - 'we recommend not setting this value and instead allowing HikariCP to act as a fixed size connection pool'; default: same as maximumPoolSize.

final_text: HikariCP's pool-sizing guide suggests connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count) as a starting point. It warns that beyond the optimum, throughput falls and response times climb.
note: Opened HikariCP wiki About-Pool-Sizing: 'connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)'; past the optimum you will 'see TPS rates starting to fall, and front-end response times starting to climb'; wants 'a small pool, saturated with threads waiting for connections'.

final_text: Amazon RDS Proxy and PgBouncer sit between app servers and the database and pool connections centrally. RDS Proxy queues or throttles client connections it cannot serve immediately, protecting the database from oversubscription during traffic surges.
note: Opened RDS Proxy guide: 'RDS Proxy queues or throttles application connections that can't be served immediately from the connection pool'; 'To protect a database against oversubscription, you can control the number of database connections'. Opened pgbouncer.org: 'lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL'.

final_text: On RDS the default max_connections is computed from instance memory: MySQL {DBInstanceClassMemory/12582880} (about MB/12; about 630 on an 8 GiB db.m7g.large), PostgreSQL LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392}, 5000).
note: Opened RDS quotas page: MySQL default {DBInstanceClassMemory/12582880} 'effectively equivalent to MB/12'; db.m7g.large example 'results in approximately 630'; PostgreSQL LEAST({DBInstanceClassMemory/9531392}, 5000). Same page: 'Database connections consume memory.'

final_text: PostgreSQL uses a process-per-connection model: for every new connection request the postmaster spawns a new backend process.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 'How Connections Are Established': 'PostgreSQL implements a process per user client/server model'; the postmaster 'spawns a new backend process every time a connection is requested'.

final_text: An AWS Application Load Balancer health-checks each target every 30 s by default and takes it out of service after 2 consecutive failures (5 successes to bring it back).
note: Opened ALB target-group health checks: HealthCheckIntervalSeconds default 30 s for instance/ip targets; HealthyThresholdCount default 5; UnhealthyThresholdCount default 2.

final_text: When Facebook built Messenger (2011), it kept a persistent connection to its servers using MQTT, a protocol chosen because it uses bandwidth and batteries sparingly.
note: Opened engineering.fb.com post (Lucy Zhang, 12 Aug 2011): 'we ended up building a new mechanism that maintains a persistent connection to our servers. To do this without killing battery life, we used a protocol called MQTT'; MQTT 'is designed to use bandwidth and batteries sparingly'. Reworded to date it as a 2011 design.

final_text: PostgreSQL's max_connections defaults to typically 100, and superuser_reserved_connections (default 3) keeps slots back for superusers, so ordinary application roles get fewer than max_connections.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 connection settings: max_connections 'default is typically 100 connections'; superuser_reserved_connections 'default value is three connections' reserved 'for connections by PostgreSQL superusers'. Reworded 'administrators' to 'superusers'; reserved_connections (default 0) can hold back more.

final_text: EC2 limits how many connections can be tracked per instance; beyond the limit packets are dropped. The conntrack_allowance_exceeded metric shows it, and with load balancers AWS recommends scaling instance count or size.
note: Opened EC2 connection tracking page: 'Amazon EC2 defines the maximum number of connections that can be tracked per instance. After the maximum is reached, any packets that are sent or received are dropped'; conntrack_allowance_exceeded metric; with ELB 'we recommend that you scale either the number of instances ... or the size of the instances'.

final_text: Redis has been benchmarked at more than 60,000 client connections while sustaining 50,000 queries/s. As a rule of thumb, 30,000 connections yield about half the throughput of 100.
note: Opened redis.io benchmarks: 'Redis has already been benchmarked at more than 60000 connections, and was still able to sustain 50000 q/s'; 'an instance with 30000 connections can only process half the throughput achievable with 100 connections.' The page does not date this benchmark; treat as an old, hardware-dependent figure.

final_text: WebSocket (RFC 6455) gives a client and server two-way communication over one connection. Before it, getting server updates meant polling the server over HTTP.
note: Opened RFC 6455: abstract 'enables two-way communication'; 1.1 'Historically, creating web applications that need bidirectional communication ... has required an abuse of HTTP to poll the server for updates'.

final_text: Redis AOF has three fsync policies: always (very slow, safest), everysec (the default; 'you may lose 1 second of data'), and no (the OS flushes, typically every 30 s on Linux). Redis recommends combining AOF with periodic RDB snapshots for backups and faster restarts.
note: Opened redis.io persistence: appendfsync always 'Very very slow, very safe'; everysec 'you may lose 1 second of data if there is a disaster'; no: 'Normally Linux will flush data every 30 seconds'; 'The suggested (and default) policy is to fsync every second'; AOF alone discouraged because 'an RDB snapshot from time to time is a great idea for doing database backups, for faster restarts'.

final_text: Redis replication is asynchronous by default; even WAIT 'does not turn a set of Redis instances into a CP system': acknowledged writes can still be lost during a failover.
note: Opened redis.io replication: 'Redis uses by default asynchronous replication'; WAIT 'does not turn a set of Redis instances into a CP system with strong consistency: acknowledged writes can still be lost during a failover'.

final_text: Redis 'expired' events are generated when Redis actually deletes the key, either on access or by an incremental background sweep, so there can be a significant delay after the TTL reaches zero. Keyspace notifications are disabled by default (notify-keyspace-events) and are fire-and-forget Pub/Sub.
note: Opened redis.io keyspace notifications: 'expired events are generated when the Redis server deletes the key and not when the time to live theoretically reaches the value of zero'; 'there can be a significant delay'; 'By default keyspace event notifications are disabled'; 'Redis Pub/Sub is fire and forget'. Also node-specific in a cluster.

final_text: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items 'typically within a few days' without consuming write capacity, and expired-but-not-yet-deleted items still show up in reads unless filtered out. Deletions appear in DynamoDB Streams as service deletions.
note: Opened DynamoDB TTL guide: 'typically within a few days after their expiration', 'without consuming write throughput', filter expressions advice, 'service deletions' in Streams. Content overlaps A-OOI-02 and A-OOI-04; optional so the page does not repeat it.

final_text: The AWS SDK for JavaScript reuses TCP connections (HTTP keep-alive) by default; AWS notes that for short operations such as DynamoDB queries, setting up a new TCP connection can cost more latency than the operation itself.
note: Opened SDK for JavaScript v3 guide: 'the AWS SDK for JavaScript reuses TCP connections by default'; 'For short-lived operations, such as Amazon DynamoDB queries, the latency overhead of setting up a TCP connection might be greater than the operation itself.' The page is JS-SDK specific, so 'AWS SDKs' generalised beyond the source; reworded.

final_text: DynamoDB typically responds in single-digit milliseconds; DAX, an in-memory cache in front of it, cuts eventually consistent reads to microseconds.
note: Opened DAX guide: 'In most cases, the DynamoDB response times can be measured in single-digit milliseconds'; DAX 'reduces the response times of eventually consistent read workloads by an order of magnitude from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds'.

final_text: In March 2024 Redis moved from its open-source licence to dual source-available licences (including SSPL), which the OSI does not accept as open source; Redis 8 (May 2025) added the OSI-approved AGPLv3 as an option. Meanwhile AWS and Google back their own fork, Valkey, which ElastiCache offers alongside Redis OSS and Memcached.
note: Opened redis.io/blog/agplv3 (Rowan Trollope, 2025-05-01): 'in March 2024, we decided to move Redis to the SSPL license'; 'AWS and Google now maintain their own fork'; 'Adding the OSI-approved AGPL as an additional licensing option for Redis, starting with Redis 8'. Opened ElastiCache What-is: 'works with the Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS engines'. Neither page states Valkey's BSD licence, so that detail was dropped.

final_text: Since Redis 8, Redis Open Source includes probabilistic types (Bloom and Cuckoo filters, Count-min sketch, Top-K, t-digest), JSON, time series and vector sets, alongside HyperLogLog and geospatial indexes.
note: Opened redis.io/blog/agplv3: Redis 8 integrates 'JSON, Time Series, probabilistic data types, Redis Query Engine and more into core Redis 8 under AGPL' and introduces vector sets. Opened data-types page: Redis Open Source lists Bloom, Count-min, Cuckoo, HyperLogLog, t-digest, Top-K, geospatial, JSON, time series, vector sets. Overlaps A-CC-16.

final_text: In InnoDB a DELETE does not physically remove the row immediately: the row and its index records are removed later by purge, once no transaction needs them for MVCC or rollback. In PostgreSQL, likewise, 'an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version'; VACUUM reclaims it.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 purge configuration: 'InnoDB does not physically remove a row from the database immediately when you delete it'; removal 'only occurs after the row is no longer required for multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) or rollback, is called a purge.' Opened PostgreSQL vacuuming: 'an UPDATE or DELETE of a row does not immediately remove the old version of the row'; reclaimed 'by running VACUUM'.

final_text: InnoDB tries to merge an index page with a neighbour only when the page's fill falls below MERGE_THRESHOLD (default 50%), after a delete or a row-shortening UPDATE. The threshold is configurable per table or per index.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 MERGE_THRESHOLD: page-full percentage below MERGE_THRESHOLD 'when a row is deleted or when a row is shortened by an UPDATE' triggers a merge attempt; 'The default MERGE_THRESHOLD value is 50'; definable 'for a table or for individual indexes'.

final_text: MySQL suggests DELETE ... LIMIT row_count, repeated until fewer rows are affected, so no single DELETE runs too long. For very large purges it also suggests copying the rows to keep into a new table and swapping it in with RENAME TABLE.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 DELETE: 'repeat the DELETE statement until the number of affected rows is less than the LIMIT value'; for many rows, copy rows not to be deleted into t_copy, then 'RENAME TABLE t TO t_old, t_copy TO t'.

final_text: PostgreSQL partial unique indexes enforce uniqueness only for rows matching a WHERE clause, e.g. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE NOT is_deleted. Soft-deleted rows then no longer block re-registration with the same email.
note: Opened PostgreSQL partial indexes: a unique partial index 'enforces uniqueness among the rows that satisfy the index predicate, without constraining those that do not' (Example 11.3, WHERE success). The users/email example is an adaptation of that pattern.

final_text: MongoDB TTL indexes are enforced by a background task in mongod that runs every 60 seconds, and under load a deletion pass can take longer, so expired documents can outlive their expiry by a minute or more.
note: Opened MongoDB TTL index manual: 'The background task that removes expired documents runs every 60 seconds'; 'expired data may exist for some time beyond the 60 second period between runs'; 'does not guarantee that expired data is deleted immediately'. The page says 'background task', not 'thread'; reworded.

final_text: In InnoDB's DYNAMIC row format (the default), long VARCHAR/TEXT/BLOB values move fully off-page behind a 20-byte pointer only when the row is too long for the page; TEXT/BLOB values of 40 bytes or less always stay inline.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 InnoDB row formats: DYNAMIC can store long variable-length values 'fully off-page, with the clustered index record containing only a 20-byte pointer'; 'Whether columns are stored off-page depends on the page size and the total size of the row. When a row is too long, the longest columns are chosen for off-page storage'; 'TEXT and BLOB columns that are less than or equal to 40 bytes are stored in line'; innodb_default_row_format default DYNAMIC.

final_text: PostgreSQL has no short/long text split: TOAST compresses or moves any wide value out of line once the row exceeds about 2 kB. Out-of-line values are fetched only if the query selects them.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 TOAST: triggered when a row 'is wider than TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD bytes (normally 2 kB)'; it will 'compress and/or move field values out-of-line'; big values 'will only be pulled out (if selected at all) at the time the result set is sent to the client'. 'No short/long text split' is the checker's inference (TOAST is size-based for any varlena type), consistent with the page.

final_text: InnoDB's maximum in-page row size is slightly under half a page (just under 8 KB with the default 16 KB pages), and MySQL caps any row at 65,535 bytes. TEXT/BLOB columns count only 9-12 bytes toward that limit because their contents are stored separately.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 column-count-limit: 'maximum row size limit of 65,535 bytes'; InnoDB max row size 'slightly less than 8KB for the default 16KB InnoDB page size'; 'BLOB and TEXT columns only contribute 9 to 12 bytes toward the row size limit'.

final_text: In MySQL, utf8mb4 characters can need up to 4 bytes, so a VARCHAR/TEXT length in characters can be up to 4x as many bytes.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 storage requirements: 'utf8mb3 and utf8mb4 character sets can require up to three and four bytes per character, respectively.'

final_text: MySQL storage sizes (5.6.4+): DATE 3 bytes, DATETIME 5 bytes, TIMESTAMP 4 bytes, plus 0-3 bytes for fractional seconds. DATETIME covers 1000-01-01 to 9999-12-31.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 storage requirements: DATE 3 bytes, DATETIME '5 bytes + fractional seconds storage', TIMESTAMP '4 bytes + fractional seconds storage', fsp 0-3 bytes. Opened datetime page: DATETIME '1000-01-01 00:00:00' to '9999-12-31 23:59:59'.

final_text: PostgreSQL timestamp and timestamptz take 8 bytes and span 4713 BC to 294276 AD at 1-microsecond resolution; date takes 4 bytes.
note: Opened PostgreSQL 18 Table 8.9: timestamp and timestamptz 8 bytes, 4713 BC to 294276 AD, 1 microsecond; date 4 bytes.

final_text: MySQL TIMESTAMP, a 4-byte epoch-based type, ends at '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC, the same Year-2038 limit that hits any signed 32-bit epoch-seconds column.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 datetime page: TIMESTAMP range ends '2038-01-19 03:14:07' UTC. PostgreSQL numeric page: integer (4 bytes) max +2147483647, the signed 32-bit limit behind 2038.

final_text: MySQL converts TIMESTAMP values to UTC for storage and back to the session time zone on retrieval, while DATETIME stores no zone at all. PostgreSQL timestamptz stores UTC and does not keep the original zone.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 datetime: 'MySQL converts TIMESTAMP values from the current time zone to UTC for storage, and back ... for retrieval. (This does not occur for other types such as DATETIME.)' Opened PostgreSQL datetime: 'the value is stored internally as UTC, and the originally stated or assumed time zone is not retained.'

final_text: SQLite has no date/time storage class: dates are stored as ISO-8601 TEXT, REAL Julian day numbers or INTEGER Unix time, and the application chooses which.
note: Opened sqlite.org datatype3 2.2: 'SQLite does not have a storage class set aside for storing dates and/or times'; TEXT ISO8601, REAL Julian day, INTEGER Unix Time; 'Applications can choose to store dates and times in any of these formats'.

final_text: India's IT Rules 2021, as summarised by the law firm Trilegal (March 2021), require intermediaries to retain information and user-registration records for 180 days for investigation purposes, and to provide information within 72 hours of receiving a lawful order.
note: Opened trilegal.com summary (dated 2 Mar 2021): 'Intermediaries must retain information and user registration records for a period of 180 days'; information to be 'provided within 72 hours from the receipt of the order'. Secondary (law-firm) source, not the gazetted Rules; later amendments to the Rules were not checked, so attributed and dated.

final_text: GDPR Art. 17 obliges organisations to erase personal data 'without undue delay' when a valid ground applies. Art. 17(3) lists exceptions such as compliance with a legal obligation and legal claims, which can justify audit retention; reusing deleted users' content for something like model training is not covered by default and needs its own legal basis or proper anonymisation.
note: Opened gdpr-info.eu Art. 17: (1) 'obligation to erase personal data without undue delay'; (3)(b) legal obligation, (3)(e) 'establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims'; (3)(d) covers archiving in the public interest and scientific/historical research only where erasure would seriously impair it. Reworded so it does not overstate: the article lists exceptions, it does not say ML archival is barred outright.

final_text: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets since 4.0 and on sharded clusters since 4.2. Its docs note that single-document operations are already atomic and that embedding often removes the need for transactions.
note: Opened MongoDB transactions manual: featureCompatibilityVersion must be at least 4.0 (replica set) and 4.2 (sharded cluster); 'an operation on a single document is atomic'; embedding means 'multi-document transactions are not necessary for many practical use cases'. 'Since 4.0/4.2' matches those release versions.

final_text: Under GDPR Art. 12(3) the controller must act on a rights request within one month of receipt; it can extend by two further months for complex or numerous requests, but must tell the person, with reasons, within the first month.
note: Opened gdpr-info.eu Art. 12(3): 'without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request. That period may be extended by two further months where necessary'; inform the person 'within one month ... together with the reasons for the delay'.

final_text: The right to erasure is not absolute: GDPR Art. 17(3) lets an organisation keep data needed for freedom of expression, compliance with a legal obligation, public health, archiving in the public interest or scientific/historical research or statistics, or the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims.
note: Opened gdpr-info.eu Art. 17(3)(a)-(e). (d) is narrower than 'archiving or research': 'archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes', and only where erasure would make those impossible or seriously impair them; reworded.

final_text: The UK ICO says erasure must also cover backups, but backup data that cannot be overwritten at once can be put 'beyond use': not restored or used for any other purpose, and overwritten on the normal schedule. The individual must be told what happens to their data in backups.
note: Opened ICO right-to-erasure guidance: 'take steps to ensure erasure from backup systems as well as live systems'; backup data put 'beyond use' until 'it is overwritten'; be clear with individuals about what happens to their data in backups. UK GDPR guidance, used here as an interpretation of the same erasure right.

final_text: GDPR's territorial scope (Art. 3): it applies to organizations established in the EU, and to non-EU organizations that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour there.
note: Opened gdpr-info.eu Art. 3: (1) establishment in the Union 'regardless of whether the processing takes place in the Union or not'; (2)(a) 'offering of goods or services ... to such data subjects in the Union'; (2)(b) 'monitoring of their behaviour as far as their behaviour takes place within the Union'.

final_text: Atlassian's April 2022 outage was caused by a deletion script given site IDs instead of app IDs; it deleted 883 sites for 775 customers, which were restored from 30-day backups over up to 14 days (all by 18 April 2022).
note: Opened Atlassian PIR: 'the team provided the IDs of the entire cloud site where the apps were to be deleted'; 'immediate deletion of 883 sites (representing 775 customers)'; 'Backups are retained for 30 days'; 'up to 14 days'; 'all customer sites progressively restored by April 18th'.

final_text: Client libraries usually do cache compression. pymemcache's CompressedSerde, for example, zlib-compresses values longer than 400 bytes and keeps the original bytes if compression does not make them smaller.
note: Opened pymemcache serde.py: CompressedSerde defaults compress=zlib.compress, min_compress_len=400; compresses only 'if len(value) > self._min_compress_len > 0'; 'Don't use the compressed value if our end result is actually larger uncompressed.'

final_text: Redis's own compression is limited to two settings: strings in RDB snapshot files are LZF-compressed by default (rdbcompression yes), and inner list nodes can be compressed with list-compress-depth (0, meaning off, by default). Compressing large values themselves is normally left to the client.
note: Opened redis.conf (unstable branch): 'Compress string objects using LZF when dump .rdb databases? By default compression is enabled'; 'list-compress-depth 0' with '0: disable all list compression'. The config file does not state that in-memory strings are 'stored as sent', so that clause was softened.

final_text: HTTP compression (Gzip, Brotli, Zstandard) helps text such as HTML, CSS, JS and JSON. MDN advises against compressing images, audio and video again, because those formats are already compressed and the overhead can make files larger.
note: Opened Cloudflare compression docs: 'Cloudflare supports Gzip, Brotli, and Zstandard compression'; compressible types are text/html, text/css, application/javascript, application/json etc. Opened MDN Compression: compress 'all files except already compressed ones like images, audio files and videos'; recompressing 'is often counterproductive ... resulting in a larger file'.

final_text: Databases read storage in fixed-size pages, 8 kB in PostgreSQL and 16 KB by default in InnoDB, so a 15-byte read and a 1 KB read cost the same single page IO.
note: Opened PostgreSQL page layout: pages 'of a fixed size (usually 8 kB)'. Opened MySQL 8.4 InnoDB physical structure: 'The default size of an index page is 16KB.' The 'same single page IO' conclusion is the checker's inference from page-granular storage; sound.

final_text: InnoDB's buffer pool is an area of main memory that caches table and index data as it is accessed, so frequently used rows are served from RAM, not disk.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 buffer pool: 'The buffer pool is an area in main memory where InnoDB caches table and index data as it is accessed. The buffer pool permits frequently used data to be accessed directly from memory'.

final_text: A PostgreSQL materialized view stores a query's results in table form. Reads can be far faster than recomputing (the docs show 188 ms dropping to 0.117 ms), but the data is only as fresh as the last REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.
note: Opened PostgreSQL materialized views: 'persist the results in a table-like form'; example 'Execution time: 188.273 ms' vs 'Execution time: 0.117 ms'; 'the data is not always current'; refresh with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. (The page notes the example used local caching.)

final_text: HTTP/1.1 defaults to persistent connections (RFC 9112 9.3); HTTP/1.0 opened a separate TCP connection per request/response unless Keep-Alive was negotiated.
note: Opened RFC 9112 9.3: 'HTTP/1.1 defaults to the use of persistent connections'; keep-alive is an HTTP/1.0 mechanism. Opened MDN Overview: 'The default behavior of HTTP/1.0 is to open a separate TCP connection for each HTTP request/response pair.'

final_text: Keep-Alive and Connection are connection-specific headers that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 forbid; Safari refuses responses that contain them, so the header matters only for HTTP/1.x.
note: Opened MDN Keep-Alive: 'Connection-specific header fields such as Connection and Keep-Alive are prohibited in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 ... Safari ... does not load any response that contains them.' Opened RFC 9113 8.2.2: lists Keep-Alive; 'Any message containing connection-specific header fields MUST be treated as malformed'.

final_text: WebSocket is a separate TCP-based protocol, but its opening handshake is an HTTP Upgrade request (RFC 6455 1.7), so a WebSocket connection starts as HTTP.
note: Opened RFC 6455 1.7: 'Its only relationship to HTTP is that its handshake is interpreted by HTTP servers as an Upgrade request.'

final_text: HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC, and QUIC packets are carried in UDP datagrams (RFC 9000), so modern HTTP does run over UDP, with QUIC providing reliability.
note: Opened RFC 9114 abstract: 'a mapping of HTTP semantics over QUIC' (2022). Opened RFC 9000 s1: 'QUIC packets are carried in UDP datagrams'; 'QUIC provides the necessary feedback to implement reliable delivery and congestion control'.

final_text: As of October 2026, Redis Open Source documents Bloom filters, cuckoo filters, count-min sketch, t-digest, top-k and HyperLogLog as built-in probabilistic data types, along with geospatial indexes, JSON, time series and vector sets.

final_text: AWS ElastiCache bills serverless caches per GB-hour of data stored plus ElastiCache Processing Units (about 1 ECPU per KB for simple reads and writes), and node-based clusters per node-hour (checked October 2026).
note: Opened aws.amazon.com/elasticache/pricing (Oct 2026): serverless data 'billed in gigabyte-hours (GB-hrs)'; 'Reads and writes require 1 ECPU for each kilobyte (KB) of data transferred'; node-based 'billed hourly from the time a node is launched until it is terminated'.
